logline: A Norwegian teen drama rotating its protagonist each season through the same Oslo school - tackling sexual assault, homosexuality, Islam, and identity with a real-time social-media format that made it the most internationally talked-about show of 2016.

renewal.note: Four-season run concluded June 24, 2017. Creator Julie Andem confirmed the series was finished. International remakes produced in France, Germany, Italy, Spain, Belgium, Netherlands, USA and others.

bollymeter.basis: Season 1 through Eva's perspective is a promising but conventional teen drama; the real formal and thematic ambition arrives in Seasons 2 and 3.

seasons.review_body: Season 1 introduces the Hartvig Nissen school in Oslo through Eva Kviig Mohn's perspective, focusing on friendship betrayal and first relationships. The real-time social media format - clips released during the week as events supposedly happened, with texts and Instagram posts between episodes - was already present but its radical implications were not yet fully apparent. The season's 11 episodes built the ensemble and established creator Julie Andem's method: a rotating protagonist, the same world each time, different pressures. Critics in Norway recognised a distinctive approach; international attention was still limited.

bollymeter.basis: Season 2 through Noora's perspective - confronting sexual assault with clinical precision - won the Gullruten for Best Drama and began drawing international fan attention for its uncompromising treatment of serious topics.

seasons.review_body: Season 2 centres on Noora Saetre and makes sexual assault its organizing subject. The Gullruten Awards recognised it with Best TV Drama and Best New Programme Series. The writing's refusal to resolve trauma quickly or neatly generated significant critical discussion in Scandinavia. Internationally, fan communities were beginning to create unofficial translations - the show's social media format meant clips circulated faster than any official distribution could contain. The New Statesman would later describe SKAM as the best show on television; the Season 2 treatment of sexual violence was the evidence cited. The show's audience appreciation within Norway reached records that Season 1 had not approached.
seasons.season_over_season: Steps up from Season 1's friendship focus to a serious treatment of sexual assault - the show's ambition becomes unmistakable.

bollymeter.basis: Season 3 broke all Norwegian streaming records with 789,000 average viewers and trended globally on Tumblr and Twitter; Isak's coming-out arc was credited by LGBTQ youth as one of the most honest representations of young male homosexuality on television.

seasons.review_body: Season 3 through Isak Valtersen's perspective tracks a gay teenager in denial, and the slow process by which he accepts his own identity alongside a relationship with Even Bech Naesheim. The Norwegian streaming figures - 789,000 average viewers, breaking all national records - were matched by extraordinary international reach: Sweden logged over 25 million plays on SVT Play; fan communities in China reached 6 million total views despite censorship. On Tumblr's 2017 year-end ranking, SKAM outranked Game of Thrones and Stranger Things as the most-discussed show. The C21Media International Drama Award for Best Digital Original recognised the show's formal innovation: real-time clips and social media as narrative delivery system, not marketing supplement. Season 3 is the franchise's critical and cultural peak.
seasons.season_over_season: The coming-out arc in Season 3 delivered on every promise the first two seasons made about the format's capacity for emotional intimacy.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 10
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The Season 3 finale resolves Isak and Even's relationship after a series of crises the show handled with real clinical care for mental health. The conclusion was widely discussed as one of the most affecting LGBTQ relationship endings in contemporary television - specific, quiet, and earned.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The rooftop scene between Isak and Even - the moment the season's worth of accumulated tension resolves into something simple and true.

bollymeter.basis: Season 4 through Sana's perspective - exploring faith, identity, and belonging as a Muslim girl in Norway - received praise for its ambition, though following Season 3 was always going to be difficult.

seasons.review_body: Season 4 centres on Sana Bakkoush, a Norwegian-Moroccan Muslim navigating faith, belonging, and prejudice among her Oslo schoolmates. Julie Andem and the writers engaged with Islamophobia, cultural identity, and the experience of being visibly different in a liberal Scandinavian environment. Dagbladet praised the handling of a conversation about religion as reflected, respectful, and enlightening. The Peer Gynt Prize was awarded to Andem in 2017 for positive impact on Norwegian society and culture internationally. Prince William and Catherine visited Hartvig Nissen School in February 2018 to meet the cast and discuss the show's youth mental health impact, a measure of the series' cultural reach far beyond its original NRK platform.
seasons.season_over_season: Shifts to religious and cultural identity after Season 3's intimate LGBTQ arc - ambitious and respectful, though Season 3's highs are not matched.
